content: ORCON, which stands for Operational Research Consultancy, was established in 1974 by a UK-based consultancy firm. It was designed as a standardized framework to evaluate and monitor the performance of ambulance services. Over time, this standard was adopted internationally, including by ambulance services in Australia. The ORCON standards are assessed using specific key performance indicators (KPIs): 1. Activation Time: For all emergency calls, an ambulance must be activated within three minutes of the call being answered. This process typically involves the control room assigning the task to the ambulance crew within one minute, followed by the crew being on the road within an additional two minutes. This target is expected to be achieved in 95% of calls. 2. Category A Calls: These are calls classified by the Advanced Medical Priority Dispatch System (AMPDS) as immediately life-threatening. For these calls: 75% must receive an initial response within eight minutes of the operator answering the call. 95% must receive an initial response within 19 minutes. The performance of the ambulance service in meeting these targets is expressed as a percentage of calls that meet the specified timeframes. 3. Category B Calls: These are calls classified by AMPDS as serious but not immediately life-threatening. For these calls: 95% must receive an initial response within 19 minutes. Similar to Category A, the performance is measured as a percentage of calls meeting this standard. Previously, there was a distinction between urban and rural ambulance services in terms of response times. Until April 1, 2006, 95% of incidents in urban areas had to be responded to within 14 minutes, while rural areas had a 19-minute target. However, this distinction was abolished, and all ambulance services are now held to the same response time requirement of 19 minutes.
